title: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms
capsule: The Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period (907–979) was a phase of political fragmentation following the collapse of the Tang dynasty, during which five short-lived dynasties (Later Liang, Later Tang, Later Jin, Later Han, Later Zhou) ruled northern China in succession while ten regional kingdoms flourished in the south and northwest. The Later Zhou emperor Chai Rong (r. 954–959) began reunification campaigns that were completed by his general Zhao Kuangyin, who usurped the throne in 960 to found the Song dynasty and progressively absorbed the remaining kingdoms, with the last — the Northern Han — falling in 979. The period was marked by military strongman (jiedushi) dominance, constant dynastic turnover, and a shift in political culture that the Song dynasty subsequently reformed.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The northern dynastic sequence is well documented in the official histories (Jiu Wudai Shi, Xin Wudai Shi); the southern kingdoms' frontier boundaries are reconstructed primarily from the same sources and are approximate.
